Research Brief · Consumer Trends

# 2026 Consumer Trends: A Mature Market Rewards Convenience and Value

Published October 29, 2026 · CannActuality Research Desk · For licensed vendors and product teams

### Key takeaways

- California — the largest US legal market — did about $311 million in tracked sales in April 2026, down 7.1% year over year, with the average item price down to $17.91 from $18.89 (Headset data).

- Pre-rolls passed flower in 2025 to become the top US cannabis category by units: an estimated $3.6 billion across 383+ million units, a 15.9% share of total sales (Custom Cones USA 2026 report, Headset data).

- Beverages were the only major California category growing in April 2026: +8.0% in sales and +14.6% in units year over year.

- The development signal: convenience formats, clear value ladders, and infused/premium variants inside proven formats — not novelty for its own sake.

## The headline: maturity, not collapse

California's legal market is large and getting harder. Tracked sales reached roughly $311 million across more than 17.3 million units in April 2026, yet sales were down 7.1% versus April 2025 and the average item price fell from $18.89 to $17.91, according to Headset market data reported by KOLAS. California still outsold every other tracked state that month. The correct read for product teams is not retreat — it is that growth now has to be taken from competitors and adjacent categories, not from a rising tide.

Price pressure is structural: more licensed competition, persistent unlicensed supply, and shoppers who compare menus before they visit. Products that cannot explain their price on the label — format, strength, count, provenance — lose to products that can.

## Where the units went: pre-rolls took the crown

The single largest format shift in US cannabis is complete. Custom Cones USA's 2026 market report, built on Headset data, found that pre-rolls passed flower for the first time in 2025 to become the top cannabis category by units, generating an estimated $3.6 billion in revenue across more than 383 million units — a 15.9% share of total sales. Pre-roll unit sales rose 18.6% year over year while the broader market grew just 1.5%, and the category's revenue has more than doubled since 2021.

Inside the category, the growth is concentrated, not uniform:

- Infused pre-rolls accounted for 47% of category revenue and posted the fastest growth — the premium tier inside a convenience format.

- The 1-gram single remained the top-selling product format — low-commitment trial drives the category's volume.

- Millennials accounted for nearly 44% of pre-roll revenue, making this the core working-age format, not a niche.

California's April 2026 category table shows the same gravity at state level: pre-rolls held up best among the large inhalable categories (down 2.5% year over year) while flower fell 10.6%.

## California category snapshot, April 2026 (Headset)

 CategoryApril 2026 salesYear-over-year
 Flower$96.43 million−10.6%
 Vapor pens$89.21 million−5.5%
 Pre-rolls$57.39 million−2.5%
 Edibles$38.06 million−3.8%
 Concentrates$15.43 million−9.6%
 Beverages$7.43 million+8.0%

Two details matter for developers. First, beverages grew units (+14.6%) faster than dollars (+8.0%) as the average beverage price fell from $7.52 to $7.09 — trial pricing is working, and the category is buying new drinkers. Second, every declining category still dwarfs beverages in absolute dollars. The opportunity is asymmetric: small base, real growth, low shelf commitment.

## What this means for product teams

- Lead with ready-to-use formats. The unit crown belongs to pre-rolls. If your roadmap is flower-first, it is fighting the last market. Singles for trial, multi-packs for regulars, infused variants for margin.

- Build an explicit value ladder. With the average item at $17.91 and falling, every SKU needs a legible rung: entry, core, premium. Unpriced ambiguity reads as overpriced.

- Treat beverages as a development priority, not a side project. The only growing major category in the largest market deserves formulation resources now — see our beverage deep-dive (thc-beverages-deep-dive.html) for strength, format, and channel specifics.

- Differentiate inside proven formats. Infused pre-rolls at 47% of category revenue show where premiumization works: upgrades to formats consumers already buy, not untested formats they must be taught.

- Plan for a flat market. A −7.1% headline in California and +1.5% national unit growth mean share-taking math: your launch case should name whose sales you are taking.

### Go deeper — the dataset behind this brief

Several figures in this brief come from BDSA retail sales tracking. If your team needs the underlying dataset — category, brand, and market-level sales to cut your own roadmap numbers — BDSA (https://bdsa1.referralrock.com/l/TAYLORAUGU09/) is the source the research cites. Research Brief · Regulatory

# The December 11 Readiness Brief: Converting Hemp SKUs to Licensed Channels

Published November 11, 2026 · CannActuality Research Desk · For licensed vendors and product teams

### Key takeaways

- Two federal dates, one direction. Hemp-derived products with cannabinoids the plant cannot naturally produce lose hemp status on November 12, 2026. The rest of the redefinition, including the 0.3% total-THC standard (THCA counted) and the 0.4 mg total-THC cap per container, takes effect December 11, 2026 (Congressional Research Service).

- California's licensed channel does not take hemp yet. Until new rules are adopted, the Department of Cannabis Control (DCC) says licensed manufacturers may use only cannabinoids from licensed sources, licensed distributors cannot transport hemp, and licensed retailers cannot sell hemp products. Hemp entry into the licensed supply chain begins January 1, 2028.

- So "conversion" in California means reformulation. A hemp SKU becomes a licensed SKU by being remade from licensed-source cannabis by a DCC-licensed manufacturer, then tested, tracked, packaged, labeled and taxed like any other cannabis product.

- Other states split three ways. Illinois folds intoxicating hemp into its cannabis law on November 12, 2026; Washington and New York already route detectable-THC products through licensees; Texas and Florida have no adult-use channel to migrate into.

- Still open: FDA's cannabinoid lists had not been published as of October 28, 2026, bills to delay or repeal the redefinition had not passed, and California's integration rules are still being written.

## The federal clock, re-verified

Section 781 of Public Law 119-37 rewrote the federal hemp definition around a total-THC concentration "including tetrahydrocannabinolic acid" of not more than 0.3% on a dry weight basis, and excluded several classes of product: those with cannabinoids not capable of being naturally produced by the plant, those with natural cannabinoids synthesized or manufactured outside the plant, and final products containing more than 0.4 mg combined total THC (and similar-effect cannabinoids) per container. CRS notes that "container" means the innermost packaging in direct contact with the product. Excluded products are classified as marijuana under the Controlled Substances Act.

The Continuing Appropriations and Extensions Act, 2027 (Public Law 119-103) delayed most of those amendments to December 11, 2026. The exclusion for cannabinoids the plant cannot naturally produce stays on November 12, 2026. CRS's October 28, 2026 Legal Sidebar reports that FDA had published none of the four items the law required (lists of naturally occurring, THC-class and similar-effect cannabinoids, plus guidance on "container"), and that bills to delay the definition by two more years (H.R. 7024, H.R. 7010, S. 3686) or to repeal it (H.R. 6209) were pending. None had been enacted as of that date. Plan to December 11.

## California first: what the licensed channel actually requires

AB 8 (Chapter 248, Statutes of 2025) was signed October 2, 2025, and most provisions took effect January 1, 2026. Since then, hemp flower and hemp pre-rolls cannot be sold in California, and the DCC lists five product types as prohibited: alcoholic beverages containing hemp cannabinoids, inhalable hemp products (pre-rolls, vape cartridges, integrated vaporizers), hemp flower, products with synthetic cannabinoids, and products made outside the regulated market. Food, beverages and dietary supplements made with industrial hemp extract may not contain THC or synthetic cannabinoids; the one remaining ingredient lane is CBD or CBN isolate above 99% purity, which still needs a CDPH registration. Tobacco retailers may not possess or sell cannabis at their locations (Business and Professions Code § 22980.6, per Kight Law).

The important detail for migration planning is the DCC's interim position: licensed manufacturers "can only use cannabinoids from licensed sources," licensed distributors "cannot transport hemp," and licensed retailers "cannot sell hemp products." Full integration on January 1, 2028 changes that. From then, distributors may bring hemp plant material into the supply chain under cannabis rules, anyone making intoxicating cannabinoid products in California needs a DCC manufacturing license, and retailers may sell products containing cannabis, hemp or both.

A brand moving into California's licensed market before 2028 is therefore entering the existing MAUCRSA system, not a hemp variant of it:

- Inputs: cannabinoids sourced from licensed operators only; no hemp-derived or synthetic inputs.

- Manufacturing: production by a DCC-licensed manufacturer.

- Testing: every batch tested by a licensed laboratory before sale, covering cannabinoids and terpenes, residual solvents and processing chemicals, pesticides, heavy metals, microbial impurities, mycotoxins, moisture content and water activity, and foreign material. Labs upload the certificate of analysis to track-and-trace within one day of finishing a batch.

- Distribution: a licensed distributor arranges testing and may transport goods to retail only if they pass; Type 11 distributors also run a quality-assurance review.

- Track-and-trace: California's system runs on Metrc, and the label must carry the system-issued UID.

- Labeling: primary panel with product identity, net weight or volume, and the universal symbol (at least 0.5 inch tall), plus "Cannabis-Infused" on edibles; informational panel with the government warning, UID, batch or lot number, packaging date, ingredients and licensee contact; THC and CBD content per package (and per serving where applicable).

- Excise tax: 15% of gross receipts on retail sales, effective October 1, 2025 (CDTFA). The rate can next be adjusted for fiscal year 2028-29, capped at 19%. CDTFA says the excise tax reaches hemp-concentrate products (other than CBD-isolate-only products) from January 1, 2028.

The state is building the 2028 bridge now. The DCC's January 9, 2026 budget change proposal asks for 22 positions and $7.3 million in 2026-27, with rulemaking to start in 2026-27 and finish in 2027-28. It also seeks $800,000 for Metrc changes to allow hemp entry and exit, which it estimates will take about 12 months, and new laboratory capacity to detect synthetic cannabinoids. A budget request is not an enacted rule, so the 2028 details remain pending.

## State-by-state checklist

 StateLicensed path for an intoxicating hemp SKUStatus and open questions
 CaliforniaReformulate on licensed-source cannabis; DCC-licensed manufacturer; licensed lab testing; Metrc UID; DCC labeling; licensed distributor and retailer; 15% excise at retail.Interim rules in force since January 1, 2026. Hemp enters the licensed chain January 1, 2028; DCC rulemaking pending.
 IllinoisSB 3222 (signed June 12, 2026) reclassifies intoxicating hemp as cannabis under the Cannabis Regulation and Tax Act from November 12, 2026. Only non-intoxicating CBD products under 0.4 mg total THC may be sold outside the licensed market.Sales under 21 banned on signing. A standalone processor license was created; 45 infuser licenses may be issued in January 2027 to applicants with social equity experience. Whether hemp-derived inputs can be used by licensed processors is not addressed in the sources reviewed.
 New YorkThe Adult-Use Processor Type 3 (Branding) license lets a brand white-label through licensed processors without a New York premises; it is one of the only application types currently open. Track-and-trace runs on Metrc.OCM says the federal law does not replace New York's cannabinoid hemp framework but may affect out-of-state products, and that management of the transition is uncertain.
 WashingtonOnly licensed cannabis retailers may sell products with any detectable THC. CBD is the only cannabinoid that may enter the licensed system from outside, and only if tested and verified below 0.3% THC.Semi- or fully synthetic conversion is prohibited in the licensed market (WSLCB, July 2026). Hemp-derived THC has no licensed entry point.
 ColoradoNo hemp entry: using hemp to make THC distillate sold as marijuana is against state law, and MED has threatened embargo, suspension or revocation and law enforcement referral.Hemp products remain capped at 1.75 mg THC per serving under SB 23-271; SB 164, which would have loosened beverage limits, was withdrawn in spring 2026. Revised MED rules on diversion and tracking took effect November 1, 2026.
 MichiganSince October 11, 2021, cannabis-derived THC products such as delta-8 are regulated by the state cannabis regulator and sold only through licensed retailers after testing and approval.SB 599-602 (consumable hemp licensing; 1.75 mg per container threshold in the Senate version) were referred to the House Regulatory Reform Committee on December 17, 2025. Later status not verified.
 Texas (contrast)No adult-use channel. The Compassionate Use Program is a medical, low-THC program; DPS is adding 12 dispensing licenses under HB 46.DSHS rules banned smokable hemp sales from March 31, 2026, added a total-THC standard counting THCA, and set a $5,000 annual retail registration per location. Spencer Fane reports delta-8 and similar converted cannabinoids stopped qualifying as hemp in Texas on July 31, 2026. Most hemp THC products fail the federal test on December 11.
 Florida (contrast)No adult-use channel; the 2026 adult-use amendment failed to qualify for the ballot (Department of State, February 2, 2026; the campaign disputed the count).State hemp-extract rules require 21+ sales, child-resistant packaging, QR-linked certificates of analysis and full-panel testing, but sit on the federal definition. No state path absorbs intoxicating hemp after December 11.

Status as of the source dates listed below. Massachusetts was not covered because no current primary source on hemp migration could be confirmed for this brief.

## What is uncertain or pending

- FDA's lists. Until FDA publishes which cannabinoids are naturally producible and THC-class, the November 12 versus December 11 sorting rests on manufacturers' own records.

- Congress. Two-year delay bills and a repeal bill were pending as of October 28, 2026. None had passed.

- California's 2028 rules. Distributor hemp endorsements, hemp testing and labeling, and Metrc entry and exit are still in rulemaking.

- Michigan and New York. Michigan's hemp package and New York's transition approach had not been resolved in the sources reviewed.

## What this means for product teams

- Inventory your hemp SKUs against both dates. Flag anything with non-naturally-producible cannabinoids for November 12 and everything above 0.4 mg total THC per container for December 11.

- In California, budget a reformulation, not a relabel. The licensed channel accepts only licensed-source cannabinoids until 2028, so plan new input sourcing, a licensed manufacturer, fresh batch testing and a new label built around the Metrc UID.

- Re-run unit economics with the 15% excise. It applies to licensed retail sales now and is scheduled to reach hemp-concentrate products in 2028.

- Pick states by entry mechanism. New York's branding license and Illinois's new processor and infuser licenses are possible routes for brands; Washington and Colorado do not admit hemp-derived THC; Texas and Florida offer no adult-use channel.

- Keep production-method records with every certificate of analysis. Washington bans synthetic conversion, Colorado treats hemp-derived inputs as a violation, and the federal sorting depends on how each cannabinoid was made.

- Watch three dockets: FDA's cannabinoid lists, the federal delay bills, and DCC's AB 8 rulemaking.

Research Brief · Category Deep-Dive

# Edibles After the Beverage Boom: Gummies, Ratios, Fast-Acting, and the Pack Ladder

Published November 11, 2026 · CannActuality Research Desk · For licensed vendors and product teams

### Key takeaways

- California edibles fell 3.8% year over year in April 2026 (Headset data). The latest month reads differently: October 2026 edible sales rose 10.0% year over year, just behind the market's 11.0% (Headset). Nationally, edibles were flat at −0.2% for the 12 months ending September 2026, holding 11.8% of US sales (Headset).

- Gummies are the category. They hold 88.6% of Colorado edible dollars (Headset, January–July 2026), and every one of California's ten best-selling edibles in Headset's October 3, 2026 snapshot was a gummy. Chocolates held 6% of edible sales in BDSA-tracked markets in Q1 2025, the same share as beverages.

- The growth is in ratios, not in THC-only products. California minor-cannabinoid edibles grew 8.2% to $115.2 million in January–August 2026 while THC-only edibles were flat. In Colorado, THC-only edibles fell 14.1% while multi-cannabinoid products grew 0.7% (Headset).

- Fast-acting is a small but concentrated premium rung. It was 3% of a $2.57 billion US gummy market in 2024 (BDSA data, in a report co-presented with a fast-acting technology vendor), yet fast-acting SKUs make up 29.4% of one gummy brand's October 2026 sales (Headset).

- Most of the market buys the same core pack: 100 mg in ten pieces. Development money earns its return by building clear rungs around that pack, through more pieces per pack, a ratio or need-state formula, or a fast-acting format, rather than by adding more THC-only flavors.

## The headline number, in context

The figure that started this brief checks out. Headset data reported by KOLAS (May 21, 2026) shows California edible sales of $38.06 million in April 2026, down 3.8% year over year. The whole market fell 7.1% that month, so edibles held up better than flower (−10.6%) and concentrates (−9.6%). The Marijuana Herald (May 5, 2026), also using Headset data, confirms the $38 million April figure.

That single month is now out of date, and the more recent numbers are better. Headset's California market page (data snapshot November 9, 2026) puts October 2026 edible sales at $37.24 million, up 10.0% year over year. The total market rose 11.0% and beverages rose 22.3%. Over a longer window, Headset's California presentation at IgniteIt (October 7, 2026) showed edible units up 5.5% and dollars up 2.9% for January–August 2026. Units grew faster than dollars, so each unit is bringing in less revenue.

 Measure (Headset)PeriodEdibles
 California sales, year over yearApril 2026−3.8%
 California dollars / units, year over yearJanuary–August 2026+2.9% / +5.5%
 California sales, year over yearOctober 2026+10.0%
 US sales, year over year (16 state markets)12 months ending September 2026−0.2%
 US share of cannabis sales12 months ending September 202611.8%
 US share of dispensary baskets containing an edible12 months ending September 202616.9%

For product teams, the takeaway is that edibles are a large, mature category that is roughly holding its size, not one in collapse. The beverage boom did not take away edibles' growth. Edible growth simply moved into particular formulas and pack types, which the rest of this brief maps.

## Gummies are the category; chocolate is a brand play

Every recent dataset points the same way:

- Colorado: gummies are 88.6% of edible category dollars (Headset Colorado deep dive, August 20, 2026, January–July 2026 data).

- BDSA-tracked markets, Q1 2025: candy, the subcategory that includes gummies, held 79% of edible sales. Chocolates held 6%, beverages 6% and pills 5% (BDSA, April 28, 2025). BDSA counts beverages inside edibles. Even so, after years of beverage headlines, drinks were the same size as chocolate.

- California's best sellers: all ten top edibles in Headset's 30-day snapshot dated October 3, 2026 were gummies sold in 10- or 20-piece packs.

- Concentration: one brand, Wyld, accounts for roughly 15% of all US edible sales, according to Headset's edible category page (October 2025–September 2026).

Chocolate still works when the brand is built on it. About 75.4% of Kiva Chocolate's October 2026 sales came from chocolate bars in its top ten products, mostly 20-piece bars. The brand also offers higher-milligram bars where state rules allow larger packages (Headset, snapshot November 3, 2026). Taken together, the data says a new chocolate or baked line needs a brand reason to exist. A new gummy line needs a reason to be chosen over an established gummy leader.

The shopper base is broader than in most categories. Women account for 42% of edible dollars, compared with 32% of flower, and Baby Boomers and Gen X together make up more than half of edible spend (Headset). In California, Gen Z edible sales grew 18.4% in January–August 2026 (Headset, IgniteIt).

## Where the growth is: ratio and minor-cannabinoid gummies

The clearest finding in 2026 data is that THC-only edibles are flat or shrinking, while multi-cannabinoid edibles are holding or growing.

- California: minor-cannabinoid edibles (CBN, CBG, THCV, CBC) grew 8.2% to $115.2 million in January–August 2026, while THC-only edibles were flat (Headset, IgniteIt, October 7, 2026).

- Colorado: edibles fell 8.1% year over year, and Headset attributes the decline almost entirely to THC-only products, which fell 14.1%. Multi-cannabinoid products grew 0.7% and now hold 44.3% of category sales. Their share is 52.2% in Washington. Of the added cannabinoids, CBN and CBG are holding or gaining, while CBD fell 10.6% (Headset, August 20, 2026).

- California best sellers: six of the top ten edibles in Headset's October 3, 2026 snapshot contain CBN alongside THC, often with CBD as well. The top two are both ratio gummies.

- Brand level: ratio SKUs make up about 40% of Wyld's October 2026 sales. The five ratio items in its top ten are 1:1:1 CBD/CBN/THC, 2:1 THC/CBN, 1:1 CBG/THC, 1:1 CBD/THC and 20:1 CBD/THC (Headset, snapshot November 10, 2026). At Jams, 2:1:1 and 1:1:1 formulas make up 31.8% of sales (Headset, snapshot November 3, 2026).

Several leading ratio SKUs carry need-state names, so the formula and the label are developed together. When making any label or marketing claim, product teams should treat need-state naming as a regulated claims question.

## Fast-acting: small share, strong positioning

"Fast-acting" in this brief is a marketing and formulation label, tied to proprietary infusion processes such as Azuca's TiME INFUSION. It is not a claim about how a product performs. The best public sales read comes from a 2025 report co-presented by BDSA and Azuca. Azuca sells fast-acting infusion technology, so treat the framing with that interest in mind. As reported by The Marijuana Herald (May 27, 2025) and in Azuca's release (May 28, 2025), the report's figures are:

- Fast-acting gummies were about 3% of the $2.57 billion US gummy market in 2024, based on BDSA retail data across 14 markets.

- Fast-acting gummies sold at higher original and sell-through prices than conventional gummies.

- Some brands with fast-acting lines drew as much as 50% of their sales from those products.

Recent brand data supports the "small but concentrated" reading. Four fast-acting 20-piece SKUs make up 29.4% of Jams' October 2026 sales. Three items in Wana's "Quick" line make up 11.2% of that brand's sales (Headset, snapshots November 3 and November 10, 2026). Fast-acting works best as a defined premium rung inside an established gummy line, not as a standalone brand promise.

## Low potency and pack-count architecture

Pack design is limited by regulation first. In California, an edible cannabis product may contain no more than 10 mg THC per serving and 100 mg THC per package (Cal. Code Regs. tit. 4, § 17304). Headset describes the standard US edible purchase as a 100 mg pack of ten 10 mg gummies. With the THC per package capped, the main variables left are piece count and the other cannabinoids in the formula.

- Piece count is a lever: the leading fast-acting SKUs at Jams and Wana fit 100 mg into 20 pieces instead of ten. Kiva's top bars are 20-piece formats.

- Low-THC ratio products sell: Wyld's 20:1 CBD/THC 20-pack contains 10 mg of THC in total and is 4.5% of brand sales. Wana's top-ten list includes a 5:1:1:1 formula with 20 mg of THC per pack (Headset).

- Hemp channel limits: in California, AB 8 has generally treated intoxicating hemp products as cannabis since January 1, 2026. Food use of CBD or CBN isolate (above 99% purity, no THC) remains possible under CDPH authorization (CDPH AB 8 FAQ). Federally, fully synthetic cannabinoids lose hemp status on November 12, 2026. The 0.4 mg total-THC-per-container limit takes effect December 11, 2026 (Foley Hoag, September 15, 2026). Low-potency hemp gummies sold outside dispensaries need a licensed-channel plan.

## The price ladder, described structurally

This brief reports no price points. The structure of the ladder can be seen in pack design and in Headset's peer benchmarking, which compares each product against others of the same product type and package size. That method means a tier is set by format and pack, not by flavor.

 TierTypical architecture in current best sellersEvidence of where it sits
 ValueTHC-only, single-cannabinoid 100 mg packsTHC-only edibles are flat in California and down 14.1% in Colorado. California's discount rate rose from 20.3% to 23.1% of shelf value in January–August 2026 (Headset).
 Core100 mg 10-pack from a category-leading gummy brandHeadset describes this pack as the standard edible purchase. Several THC-only Wyld 10-packs rank in California's top ten.
 PremiumRatio or minor-cannabinoid 10-packs, fast-acting 20-packs, branded chocolate barsRatio items are about 40% of Wyld's sales. Headset's peer comparison places Wana's top ten above the same-type, same-pack peer average. Fast-acting sells at a premium to conventional gummies (BDSA/Azuca).

Discounting is the main risk to this ladder. When the discount rate rises, premium and core products are pushed toward value. Headset's 2026 advice to California retailers is to protect margin and increase basket attachment rather than deepen discounts.

## What this means for product teams

- Put new edible R&D money into ratio formulas, not more THC-only flavors. In both California and Colorado, multi-cannabinoid edibles held or grew while THC-only edibles stalled. CBN and CBG are the additions holding up, and CBD-only additions are fading.

- Develop gummies first. At 79% to 88.6% of edible dollars, the gummy is the default. Develop chocolate or baked goods only when your brand has a reason to own that format.

- Treat fast-acting as a defined premium rung. It holds a small share of the market but a large share of some brands' sales. Use "fast-acting" only as a marketing label, and keep any onset claims within what state rules allow.

- Build the ladder from pack architecture. Within a 100 mg cap, piece count (10 vs 20), formula (THC-only vs ratio) and format (standard vs fast-acting) are the rungs. Each SKU should have one clear reason to sit on its rung.

- Budget for a flat category with shifting mix. Plan for a US category that is about level overall. Base the launch case on taking share from THC-only basics, and update it with each month of state data. The April figures were already out of date by October.

- Close out hemp-channel exposure before December 11, 2026. Any gummy sold outside licensed dispensaries needs a documented licensed-channel path or an exit plan.

Research Brief · Cultivation Science

# Lighting Science for Cultivation: Spectrum, Intensity, and Product Consistency

Published November 9, 2026 · CannActuality Research Desk · For licensed vendors and product teams

### Key takeaways

- Intensity is the yield dial, not the potency dial. In the Guelph trials, dry inflorescence yield rose linearly with canopy PPFD up to 1,800 µmol·m⁻²·s⁻¹, and a high-THC cultivar produced 1.6 times the inflorescence dry weight at 1,000 versus 600 µmol·m⁻²·s⁻¹ — while cannabinoid concentration did not move with intensity in either study. Grams are bought with photons; percentage points are set mainly by genetics and spectrum.

- Spectrum moves chemistry at the margins, and the direction depends on the cultivar. Blue-rich light raised CBGA, the central cannabinoid precursor, in the Bernstein group's work; LED spectra raised THC and CBD concentrations relative to HPS in a repeated head-to-head trial, while HPS produced more flower mass; and end-of-day far-red raised THC concentration in two high-THC lines. No spectrum recipe transfers across cultivars untested.

- UV is the most oversold dial in the grow room. Two controlled programs found no change in inflorescence cannabinoid content from added UV. The one positive result is narrow: low-dose, UVA-dominant light lifted linalool by 29%, limonene by 25% and myrcene by 22%, with yield and cannabinoid concentration unchanged (Huebner et al., 2024).

- Photoperiod is a consistency variable, not a fixed constant. Across three medicinal cultivars, schedules starting at 14 hours of light produced the highest flower biomass in every line — but a static 14-hour day significantly reduced THC concentration in the two THC lines while raising the CBD line's total CBD yield by 50–100% (Peterswald et al., 2023). Batch consistency starts with one locked recipe per cultivar.

## LED vs HPS: a redistribution, not a verdict

The cleanest head-to-head remains a 2018 Italian trial. Magagnini, Grassi and Kotiranta grew clones of the drug-type cultivar G-170 under three spectra at the same canopy intensity — about 450 µmol·m⁻²·s⁻¹ — on an 18-hour vegetative and 12-hour flowering schedule: high-pressure sodium (HPS) and two LED spectra, Valoya's AP673L and NS1. Then they repeated the entire experiment. HPS produced taller plants and more flower dry weight. Both LED treatments produced higher THC and CBD concentrations, and NS1 the highest CBG content. Total cannabinoid yield per plant did not differ significantly between the three light sources, and the pattern was similar in both runs.

Read carefully, that is evidence that spectrum redistributes output between flower mass and concentration — the two numbers a biomass buyer prices separately. A cultivation partner who swaps HPS for LED, or the reverse, between contract cycles can move the certificate of analysis and the kilogram count in opposite directions without changing genetics, feed or room. A 2021 Frontiers in Plant Science review of the spectrum literature adds the compound-specific caveat: visible LED light can augment THC and terpene accumulation, but not CBD. There is no general "quality" direction from a fixture change — only per-compound responses that have to be measured cultivar by cultivar.

## Blue, green and far-red: three different levers

Blue:red ratio. Danziger and Bernstein's 2021 trial in Industrial Crops and Products — its findings summarized in the Frontiers review — varied the blue:red ratio across three medical cannabis cultivars. Blue-rich light stimulated accumulation of CBGA, the central precursor from which THCA, CBDA and CBCA are made, relative to far-red-rich HPS light; the downstream cannabinoids responded less strongly and in cultivar-specific ways, and blue light was the most effective lever for keeping plants compact. Namdar and colleagues' rich-blue flowering treatment likewise raised CBGA content and the CBGA:THCA ratio. The discipline point for product teams: a precursor shift is not a finished-potency guarantee. What reaches the certificate of analysis depends on how each cultivar converts CBGA onward.

Green light and the lower canopy. Hawley's 2018 subcanopy work, as reviewed in Frontiers in Plant Science, put light inside the canopy rather than above it. Blue+red and blue+green+red subcanopy treatments both raised Δ9-THC content and CBGA levels, and the green-containing treatment had the stronger effect on terpene accumulation in both the upper and the lower canopy. This matters because light intensity falls steeply with distance from the fixture — in the Guelph intensity work, small changes in distance from the source produced substantial differences in leaf-level light — so the bottom of a tall plant grows in a different light environment from the top. Spectrum decisions are usually made for the top of the canopy; the chemistry of the lower canopy is where within-batch variance is manufactured.

Far-red as a timed signal. Far-red light (roughly 700–750 nm) works through the phytochrome system: a falling red:far-red ratio is the plant's shade signal, triggering elongation. Peterswald and colleagues (Scientific Reports, 2025) tested whether end-of-day far-red could substitute for full-spectrum hours in three medicinal cultivars. Adding 2 hours of far-red in darkness after a 10-hour day raised total cannabinoid yield in Northern Lights by nearly 70% over the 12-hour control (0.43 vs 0.25 g per plant), far-red treatments elevated THC concentration in both high-THC varieties, and that schedule used 5.5% less power than 12 hours of full light. Dose discipline is the catch: 4 hours of far-red layered onto a full 12-hour photoperiod significantly reduced trimmed flower weight in all genotypes. Far-red is a signal applied at a specific time of day — not a background ingredient to blend into a spectrum and forget.

## UV: strong claims, narrow evidence

The popular claim — add ultraviolet light, raise THC — has been tested in two modern controlled programs and failed in both. Llewellyn and colleagues (Frontiers in Plant Science, 2022) grew the high-THC cultivar Meridian at 600 µmol·m⁻²·s⁻¹ with either UVA added across flowering or UVA+UVB for the last 20 days. There were no UV effects on any biomass metric and no effects on inflorescence cannabinoid concentrations. The single positive signal sat in the sugar leaves, where UVA+UVB raised THC concentration by about 30% without changing the total THC held in that tissue — a shift inside a trim fraction, not a potency gain in flower. The authors' conclusion is blunt: no commercially relevant benefits of adding UV to indoor production. An earlier UVB study they discuss, using short-wave 287 nm LEDs, found only deleterious effects on morphology, physiology, yield and quality.

Huebner and colleagues (Frontiers in Plant Science, 2024) ran the most granular UV trial to date — three UV spectra at five intensities on the CBD cultivar Fedora 17 — and found the same null for cannabinoids: no UV treatment altered the cannabinoid profile. One treatment did move terpenes. The lowest-dose, UVA-dominant variant (99:1 UVA:UVB at 1.81 W/m²) raised linalool by 29%, limonene by 25% and myrcene by 22% versus the no-UV control, at constant yield and cannabinoid concentration. Higher UVB shares shrank leaf area, and the authors judged only that one low-dose variant suitable for practical use in commercial cultivation. On current evidence, UV is a narrow terpene tool with a dose ceiling — not a potency tool.

## Intensity and DLI: photons buy grams

Intensity is the best-documented lever in this literature. Rodriguez-Morrison, Llewellyn and Zheng (Frontiers in Plant Science, 2021) grew cannabis across canopy PPFDs from 120 to 1,800 µmol·m⁻²·s⁻¹ through a 12-week flowering period: dry inflorescence yield increased linearly across the entire range, and apical inflorescence density and harvest index rose with it — more light meant more flower, and a larger share of the plant that was saleable flower. Cannabinoid potency showed no response to intensity; terpene potency shifted only slightly. Llewellyn's 2022 trial found the same shape over a commercial range in a high-THC cultivar: moving from 600 to 1,000 µmol·m⁻²·s⁻¹ — the 600 level corresponds to a daily light integral (DLI) of 25.9 mol·m⁻²·d⁻¹ under 12 hours — made inflorescence dry weight 1.6 times higher, other biomass metrics 1.3–1.5 times higher, and harvest index 7% higher, again with no change in cannabinoid concentration.

One hemp result cuts the other way, and it is worth keeping in view precisely because it breaks the pattern. In a 2025 Frontiers in Plant Science vertical-farm trial, raising white-LED intensity from 200 to 600 µmol·m⁻²·s⁻¹ during flowering raised total CBD in the hemp cultivar Queen Dream by about 37%, alongside coordinated upregulation of cannabinoid-pathway genes, including CBDAS. It was a small trial, in a different chemotype and production system from the drug-type studies — which is the point. Whether intensity moves potency is a per-cultivar question, not a law. What is consistent across every program is the input side: the crop is responding to total photons delivered, PPFD multiplied by hours (the DLI), so the commercial question is grams per unit of light delivered — and the energy and infrastructure that light requires — not maximum light for its own sake.

## Photoperiod and the consistency problem

Photoperiod is usually treated as a fixed industry constant: 18 hours to vegetate, 12 to flower. Peterswald and colleagues (Plants, 2023) tested nine flowering schedules across three medicinal cultivars — static 10-, 12- and 14-hour days plus mid-flower switches of two and four hours. Treatments starting at 14 hours produced the highest flower biomass in all three lines. But in the two high-THC lines, a static 14-hour day significantly reduced THC concentration, while in the CBD line Cannatonic the 14-hour starts raised CBD concentration enough to lift total CBD yield by 50–100%. The authors conclude that the assumption that 12:12 is optimal for all lines is incorrect. For product teams, the same finding doubles as a consistency warning: one facility-wide schedule change is a yield improvement for one cultivar and a potency change for another.

That is the thread connecting every section of this brief. Where researchers held a light recipe constant and repeated it — Magagnini's duplicate runs are the clearest case — spectrum effects reproduced. Variance enters when the recipe moves: a fixture swap, a dimming or schedule change, a spectrum experiment rolled out across cultivars it was never tested on, or a canopy gradient nobody changed on purpose. A brand buying biomass sees the end of that chain on a certificate of analysis. Unexplained COA drift between batches is, very often, a lighting recipe that drifted first — in the grow room, weeks earlier, and auditable only if the recipe was written down.

## What this means for product teams

- Buy the recipe, not the fixture. Require cultivation partners to record, per cultivar, the spectrum class, canopy PPFD or DLI, and photoperiod — and to treat any change to those as a process change. A fixture swap, a new dimming profile or a schedule adjustment should trigger comparative certificates of analysis on the first batch under the new recipe before it ships against the old specification.

- Price intensity as yield, never as potency. For drug-type cannabis, the controlled evidence is consistent: more photons buy grams and harvest index, linearly to very high PPFD, at flat cannabinoid concentration. A supplier pitch that ties a lighting upgrade to higher THC percentage needs that supplier's own per-cultivar trial data behind it.

- Ask UV users for the waveband, the dose and their COAs. Added UV showed no cannabinoid benefit in two controlled programs, and the one positive result is low-dose UVA lifting specific terpenes (linalool, limonene, myrcene) at constant cannabinoids. If a growing partner runs UV, those three items are the diligence — a fixture name is not.

- Pilot every spectrum or schedule change on one cultivar first. Blue-rich spectra, end-of-day far-red and longer photoperiods all produced genotype-dependent effects — in the photoperiod work, opposite in sign between THC and CBD lines. One room, one cultivar, with COAs, is the unit of evidence; rolling a recipe out on another cultivar's data is how COA drift gets built into a supply contract.

- Audit the lower canopy. Light falls steeply below the top of the canopy, and subcanopy work shows chemistry differs by canopy layer. Ask how lower-canopy flower is lit, and whether it is segregated or blended at harvest. Blending policy is a consistency decision that belongs in the specification, not an afterthought at the trim table.

### Sources

Research Brief · Regulatory

# Medical-Channel Economics After Schedule III: What DEA Registration Changes for Product Teams

Published November 11, 2026 · CannActuality Research Desk · For licensed vendors and product teams

### Key takeaways

- The medical pathway is live. On October 30, 2026, the Justice Department announced DEA's first registrations under the April 2026 order: more than 900 dispensaries in Alabama, Florida, Mississippi, South Dakota, Texas, Virginia and West Virginia. Manufacturer and distributor applications are still under review.

- November 29, 2026 is the next hard date. DEA guidance expects "timely applicants" to source only from other timely applicants or registrants by then. Every medical SKU's inputs now carry a federal status question.

- Labeling stays state-led, with one federal addition. Registrants may follow state packaging and labeling rules, plus the 21 U.S.C. § 825(c) anti-transfer warning "where applicable."

- § 280E relief has been promised but not issued as formal guidance. Treasury and the IRS have previewed relief for medical activity, but as of November 11, 2026 we found no published notice or regulation. Model both outcomes.

- Broader rescheduling is still undecided. The ALJ's stay ran out on its own terms when reply briefs closed on November 5, 2026. We found no recommended decision as of today.

## What the order did, and what it did not do

The final order (AG Order No. 6754-2026) was signed April 22 and announced April 23. It was published and took effect on April 28, 2026 (91 Fed. Reg. 22714). It relies on 21 U.S.C. § 811(d)(1), the treaty-based authority, and amends 21 C.F.R. parts 1300, 1301, 1308 and 1312. It adds three categories to Schedule III at 21 C.F.R. § 1308.13(g):

- marijuana in an FDA-approved product or subject to a state medical marijuana license;

- marijuana extract under the same two conditions;

- naturally derived delta-9 THC under the same conditions, with hemp excluded.

Several categories stay in Schedule I: unlicensed bulk material, synthetically derived THC (the order gives delta-10 THC as an example) and anything non-medical. New § 1301.13(k)(1)(iv) says registrations "do not authorize the manufacture, distribution, dispensing, or use of marijuana" for non-medical purposes. A "state medical marijuana license" is a license issued by a state, D.C. or territorial entity that authorizes manufacturing, distribution or dispensing for medical purposes.

## The registration pathway: 21 C.F.R. § 1301.13(k)

 ElementWhat the rule says
 Registration typesManufacturer (cultivate, produce, process, package, label, transfer), distributor and dispenser. One entity may hold more than one type.
 State licenseTreated as "conclusive evidence" of state authorization. The registration cannot exceed the license's scope. It is suspended automatically if the license is suspended, revoked or expires.
 Expedited reviewDEA will "make every effort" to process applications filed within 60 days of publication (April 28–June 26, 2026) within six months. Those applicants may keep operating under their state license while the application is pending.
 Records and reportsLimited to what federal statute and treaty obligations require. State-required reports, records and forms are accepted "to the maximum extent permissible."
 Labeling and packagingRegistrants are exempt from the federal labeling, packaging and sealing requirements of 21 C.F.R. part 1302 if they follow state law. The label must also carry the § 825(c) warning "where applicable."
 Security and disposalMeeting state physical-security rules is sufficient, and disposal may follow state law.
 DispensingA state medical certification is sufficient if it is dated and signed on the day issued and names the patient and address and the practitioner's state license number.
 Treaty mechanicsManufacturers set a nominal crop price. DEA buys the crop at that price and resells it at the same price plus an administrative fee. Crops must be stored where DEA can inspect them, and the registration specifies cultivation areas.

Section 825(c) requires a warning on Schedule II–IV drugs dispensed to a patient that "it is a crime to transfer the drug to any person other than the patient." The order does not define "where applicable."

## Implementation since October 30

DOJ calls the October 30 dispensary registrations a "first phase." Manufacturer and distributor applications still need facility inspections, production controls and quota decisions. DOJ adds that state licensure alone does not guarantee registration, and that registrants must meet federal security, recordkeeping and inventory-control requirements.

DEA's "Timely Applicant Information for Medical Marijuana Applicants" (October 30, 2026) sets the supply-chain rule. According to reporting by Cannabis Business Times and Foley Hoag:

- Timely applicants may transact only with other timely applicants and registrants, and must check the status of their counterparties.

- They are expected to have compliant supply chains by November 29, 2026.

- Dispensaries and distributors may sell through inventory acquired before the guidance, even from non-qualifying sources. Foley Hoag notes that this allowance is not expressly extended to manufacturers.

- DEA does not plan to penalize sending small quantities to unregistered state-licensed testing labs.

Foley Hoag notes that the guidance does not have the force of law. DEA has also proposed denying a Minneapolis dispensary's application on three grounds:

- Minnesota's dual-purpose license is not a "state medical license" with robust protections against diversion;

- veterans may self-attest to qualifying status;

- the state allows dispensing of synthetic and artificially derived cannabinoids, which remain in Schedule I.

Two legal tracks remain open. On September 9, 2026, the D.C. Circuit denied a motion to stay the medical order. That keeps the order in force, but the merits are undecided. Harris Sliwoski expects a ruling no earlier than about March 2027.

In the broader rescheduling proceeding, Chief ALJ Derek C. Julius admitted the GAO report and denied a request to reopen the hearing on October 22. He allowed limited briefs, due October 29, with replies due November 5. His order said the stay "will expire by its own terms at the conclusion of this briefing schedule." We found no recommended decision as of November 11.

## Which medical programs are most exposed

Cannabis Business Times reports DEA's timely-applicant list at nearly 7,000 applicants: 4,197 dispensaries, 2,086 manufacturers and 710 distributors. The largest state pools are shown below.

 StateTimely applicantsStatus note
 Oklahoma2,442Largest pool; not among the first seven registration states
 Florida812First-phase dispensary registrations issued
 California771Medical and adult-use licensing; DCC lets licensees change A/M designation
 Maine320No first-phase registrations
 Pennsylvania227No first-phase registrations
 Missouri209No first-phase registrations

Foley Hoag describes the seven first-phase states as medical-only markets, and notes that Virginia has not yet begun adult-use licensing. The supply rule bites hardest where few upstream businesses applied. Harris Sliwoski notes Iowa appears to have only two applicants and warns that "without registered cultivators, dispensaries will lack a lawful source of marijuana." In Minnesota, 30 businesses applied, and more than 300 dispensary licensees did not.

## Dual-licensed operators: the split-portfolio problem

The order does not address co-located or shared medical and adult-use operations. Foley Hoag's reading is that "adult-use activity falls entirely outside the federal registration framework," and that DEA has not said how much separation is enough. The practical questions depend on how each state licenses the two channels:

- Single combined licenses. In states such as Minnesota, it is unclear whether an operator can register at all. Harris Sliwoski notes that a product's medical or adult-use status there is not settled until the point of sale.

- Separate or separable licenses. California's DCC emergency rules let licensees change A/M designation at any time and created a path to split combined A/M retail licenses on the same premises. New Jersey restricts medical product from moving into adult-use retail.

- Traceability. Foley Hoag advises that operators be able to show through inventory tracking that medical product stays in designated channels. Dickinson Wright lists as still open whether medical inventory can ever return to adult-use channels.

## The § 280E question: what is and is not settled

This section is research, not legal or tax advice. Section 280E positions should be decided with qualified tax counsel.

What the official record says. The order states that state licensees "will no longer be subject to the deduction disallowance imposed by Section 280E." It also says "nothing in this rule constitutes a determination regarding federal tax liability," and it encourages Treasury to consider retrospective relief.

Treasury's April 23, 2026 release says rescheduling "generally removes" § 280E for activity that no longer involves Schedule I or II substances. It says relief generally applies for the full taxable year that includes the order's effective date. It also says guidance will clarify that, for businesses with more than one activity, § 280E applies only to the Schedule I/II activity, for example by apportioning expenses. Adult-use activity remains Schedule I.

What is not settled.

- No formal guidance yet. The IRS's 2026–2027 Priority Guidance Plan (September 29, 2026) lists "Guidance under §280E," but we found no notice or regulation published as of November 11.

- Whether registration is required. Holland & Hart sets out two readings: relief follows from the scheduling change alone, or unregistered handling remains federally prohibited and keeps § 280E in play.

- How expenses are apportioned between medical and adult-use activity.

- Prior years. In New Mexico Top Organics v. Commissioner (Tax Court Docket No. 19661-24, pending), the IRS continues to reject non-280E positions, according to Foley Hoag.

- Litigation risk. Holland & Hart notes that if the D.C. Circuit vacates the order, § 280E "could be back."

 Outcome A: relief as previewedOutcome B: relief narrowed, delayed or reversed
 Tax treatmentMedical activity deducts ordinary expenses for the full 2026 taxable year. Dual operators apportion, and adult-use remains under § 280E.Guidance ties relief to registration, takes a strict view of apportionment, or the order is vacated. § 280E continues for some or all medical activity.
 Portfolio effectAfter-tax margin on medical-designated SKUs improves relative to adult-use SKUs. Clean channel attribution becomes a financial asset.Medical-specific SKUs must justify themselves on pre-tax economics and patient demand alone.
 Planning stanceBuild SKU-level cost allocation now so apportionment can be supported.Avoid medical-only investments whose payback depends on the deduction.

The same work serves both outcomes: clean medical/adult-use attribution at SKU and cost-center level.

## What this means for product teams

- Audit every medical SKU's inputs before November 29. List each input (flower, biomass, distillate, co-packer, white-label partner) and its counterparty's timely-applicant or registration status. Manufacturers should not assume they can sell through non-qualifying inventory.

- Keep medical lines to naturally derived delta-9. Synthetic and artificially derived cannabinoids remain Schedule I, and DEA cited them in the Minnesota show-cause order.

- Plan artwork for the § 825(c) warning. State rules still govern labels. Reserve space and a change process for the federal anti-transfer warning until DEA clarifies "where applicable."

- Separate medical and adult-use SKUs. Use distinct SKU codes, inventory tags and, where state rules allow, distinct packaging. Do not assume product can move between channels.

- Run two sets of numbers for § 280E. Show Outcome A and Outcome B side by side in medical-line business cases until formal IRS guidance is published.

- Watch upstream registrations. Manufacturer and distributor registrations have not been issued yet. Medical launches depend on suppliers clearing inspection and quota review.

Research Brief · Product Intelligence

# Minor Cannabinoids in Product Development: CBN, CBG, THCV and the 2026 Formulation Map

Published November 9, 2026 · CannActuality Research Desk · For licensed vendors and product teams

### Key takeaways

- Minor cannabinoids are a ratio business, not a standalone one. In BDSA's licensed-market tracking, gummies accounted for about 75% of sales dollars for CBN-containing products and about 70% for CBG-containing products — and 2026 point-of-sale data and launches show the same pattern: CBN, CBG and THCV appear inside multi-cannabinoid gummies, tablets and softgels alongside THC and CBD, not as single-cannabinoid products.

- CBG is the largest minor cannabinoid by modelled US market share — about 45% in 2024 — while CBN is the fastest-growing, at a forecast 15% CAGR (Emergen Research). THCV is the scarcest of the three: most cannabis plants yield less than 0.2% THCV, according to the Washington State Liquor and Cannabis Board's July 2026 research brief.

- How a minor cannabinoid is made is now a legal variable, not just a cost variable. Washington permits only naturally extracted THCV in its licensed market and prohibits semi-synthetic conversion. Federally, cannabinoids the plant cannot naturally produce lose hemp status on November 12, 2026; natural cannabinoids that were synthesized or manufactured outside the plant — and finished hemp products above 0.4 mg of total THC per container — follow on December 11, 2026.

- California preserves one narrow hemp lane for CBN: under AB 8, CBD or CBN isolate above 99% purity, with no THC and no synthetic cannabinoids, may still be used in foods and beverages outside the licensed system (California Department of Public Health). Everything intoxicating in California moves through licensed channels.

## The map in one view: fast growth, small base

Two kinds of evidence describe this market, and they measure different things. Emergen Research models the total US minor cannabinoid market — licensed cannabis, hemp-derived and wellness channels combined — at $1.5 billion in 2024, projected to reach $4.5 billion by 2034 at an 11.5% compound annual growth rate. That is a modelled estimate, not point-of-sale data, and its scope is deliberately broad. BDSA's Retail Sales Tracking measures the narrower licensed dispensary channel, and its most detailed public cut remains the baseline every later dataset builds on: in Q1 2022, across California, Colorado, Illinois, Massachusetts, Michigan, Nevada and Oregon, there were about 70% more products containing CBN than a year earlier, and more than twice as many products containing CBG.

The growth rates were dramatic precisely because the base was small. In the mature markets BDSA tracks separately, Q1 2022 sales of CBG-containing products rose 655% year over year in California, 1,105% in Nevada, 1,185% in Oregon and 1,251% in Colorado, while CBN-containing product sales rose 22% to 145% in the same states. In those same markets, CBD-containing product sales were still roughly three times CBN sales and more than nine times CBG sales — and CBD sales were falling by double digits. Consumer familiarity explains the headroom: BDSA consumer data put familiarity with CBN at 14% and with CBG at 13% in fall 2021, up from 11% and 8% in fall 2019. Minor cannabinoids are where formulation differentiation is happening; they are not yet where most dollars are.

 Market (BDSA, Q1 2022 vs Q1 2021)CBN productsCBG productsCBD products
 California+29%+655%−24%
 Colorado+145%+1,251%−19%
 Nevada+30%+1,105%−29%
 Oregon+22%+1,185%−17%

Sales-dollar change for products containing each cannabinoid, BDSA Retail Sales Tracking.

## Where they show up: gummies first, then tablets and softgels

The format map is unusually concentrated. In BDSA's Q1 2022 data, gummies took about 75% of sales dollars for CBN-containing products and about 70% for CBG-containing products. The next formats were an order of magnitude smaller: for CBN, chocolate and tinctures at about 5% each; for CBG, tinctures at about 10% and taffy at about 5%. A development plan that starts anywhere other than gummies is starting away from the demonstrated demand.

Current licensed-market data shows the pattern holding in 2026. Headset's October 2026 brand data for Jams — an edibles-only brand whose top 10 products account for 83.1% of its sales — lists four multi-cannabinoid ratio gummies in that top 10: a THC/CBD/CBN 2:1:1 gummy as the brand's number-one product at 17.2% of brand sales, a THC/CBG/THCV 2:1:1 gummy at 7.5%, a THC/CBD/CBG 2:1:1 gummy at 4.7%, and a CBD/CBN/THC 1:1:1 gummy at 2.4%. The ratio is printed as the product's identity; the minor cannabinoid is the differentiator inside a format buyers already understand.

The 2026 launch record adds two formats beside gummies. In October 2026, Ascend Wellness Holdings launched a seven-formula tablet line in Massachusetts, Illinois and New Jersey in which every formula pairs THC with one or more minor cannabinoids: CBN in the two nighttime-positioned formulas, THCV and CBC in the daytime-positioned formula, and CBG in three of the seven. In May 2026, Canopy Growth's Spectrum Therapeutics expanded its medical softgel lineup to 30- and 90-count packs built entirely on minor-cannabinoid ratios — CBD:CBG 1:1, CBD:CBC:CBG 2:1:1 and 5:2:2, CBD:CBN 2:1, and CBN:CBD:THC 1:1:2. Note the supporting player in both lineups: CBC, rarely headlined, appears in Ascend's THCV formula and Canopy's core daily softgel. The 2026 formulation map is therefore a ladder — gummies for reach, tablets and softgels for measured, repeatable formats — with CBN, CBG, THCV and CBC assigned by use occasion in the brand's own labelling.

A discipline note on that labelling: brand positioning is market evidence about what companies believe buyers want; it is not evidence of effect. CannActuality reports positioning as positioning. The Washington LCB's THCV brief makes the underlying point plainly — human research on THCV is limited and the bulk of the literature is preclinical — and product teams should hold the same line in their own claims review.

## Cannabinoid by cannabinoid: three different supply problems

CBN (cannabinol) — the degradation product with the clearest format fit. CBN is not a primary plant product: it forms as THC oxidizes with age, heat and light, which is why commercial supply depends on controlled conversion and purification of plant-derived material rather than on a CBN-rich harvest. Its market position is the most established of the three: BDSA found the top-selling CBN products in California, Colorado and Illinois were positioned around nighttime use, and Emergen projects CBN as the fastest-growing minor cannabinoid segment at a 15% CAGR. California's AB 8 also gives CBN a distinction no other minor cannabinoid in this brief has: CBN isolate above 99% purity, with no THC, is expressly preserved as an ingredient that can be added to foods in the state's hemp program, per the Department of Public Health.

CBG (cannabigerol) — the precursor, harvested early or bred for. CBG's acid form, CBGA, is the biosynthetic precursor the plant converts into THCA, CBDA and CBCA, so by maturity most CBGA has already been converted onward and CBG itself remains at low levels in mature plants. Commercial CBG supply therefore comes mainly from CBG-dominant hemp cultivars bred for that profile. CBG is the largest minor cannabinoid segment in Emergen's US model at about 45% share in 2024, and its licensed-market products skew to daytime-positioned ratios — BDSA's top-selling CBG product in California and Colorado was a 1:1 CBG pear gummy, and Canopy's 2026 softgel expansion leads its daytime line with a CBD:CBG 1:1 formulation.

THCV (tetrahydrocannabivarin) — the scarce varin. THCV is the propyl-side-chain counterpart of THC, produced through a separate varin pathway (from CBGVA, not CBGA). The Washington LCB's July 2026 research brief — written because the state's licensing team asked whether THCV is only available synthetically — reports that most cannabis plants yield less than 0.2% THCV, that certain African-origin cultivars such as Durban Poison are reported to test higher (while noting cultivar names are not reliable indicators and the batch certificate of analysis governs), and cites one market-research estimate valuing the US THCV market at $130 million by 2033. The LCB distinguishes Δ9-THCV, which occurs naturally, from Δ8-THCV, which has not been documented to occur naturally and is only semi-synthetically derived, typically by converting CBDV. In Washington's licensed market, only naturally occurring, in-state-extracted THCV is permitted; semi-synthetic and fully synthetic conversion are prohibited, and CBD is the only cannabinoid that may be brought in from outside the licensed system as an additive. THCV is thus a small, supply-constrained ingredient whose legal production method varies by state — the opposite of a commodity input.

## What the December 2026 federal hemp dates do to supply

The federal change is a redefinition, not a product-by-product ban list, and it sorts minor-cannabinoid supply by how the molecule was made. Section 781 of Public Law 119-37 rewrote the hemp definition around a 0.3% total-THC standard (counting THCA) and excluded three classes of hemp-derived cannabinoid products, as the Congressional Research Service summarizes in In Focus IF13136: products containing cannabinoids not capable of being naturally produced by the plant; products containing natural cannabinoids that were synthesized or manufactured outside the plant; and finished products above 0.4 mg of combined total THC per container. Products outside the definition are treated as marijuana under the Controlled Substances Act.

The September 2026 delay law (Public Law 119-103, §2019) split the effective dates. On November 12, 2026 — three days after this brief publishes — only the first class loses hemp status: cannabinoids the plant cannot naturally produce at all, with THC-O the clearest case in the legal reporting. CBN, CBG and THCV are all naturally producible, so none of them is in the November group by identity. On December 11, 2026, the rest takes effect: the total-THC test, the 0.4 mg per-container cap, and the exclusion for natural cannabinoids manufactured outside the plant. That second date is the one that reaches mainstream minor-cannabinoid supply, because a large share of hemp-derived CBN, CBG and converted THCV ingredients is produced by converting abundant hemp CBD or CBDV outside the plant rather than by extracting the target molecule directly. A hemp-derived finished product that pairs a minor cannabinoid with THC above the per-container cap also fails on December 11, regardless of how the minor itself was made.

Two uncertainties should be written into supply plans rather than assumed away. First, the statute directed FDA to publish lists of naturally producible and THC-class cannabinoids within 90 days of enactment; as of the Congressional Research Service's September 28, 2026 update, no list had been published, and industry reporting checking again in October 2026 found none — so the natural-versus-converted determination currently rests on the manufacturer's own production records and certificates of analysis. Second, bills to delay, repeal or replace the redefinition remained pending without passage as of mid-October 2026 reporting; December 11 is the planning date. What does not change: products made and sold inside state-licensed cannabis and medical systems are not hemp products, and the redefinition does not alter their status — which is why the licensed channel is the stable home for minor-cannabinoid formulation work in 2027, with hemp-derived supply requalifying ingredient by ingredient on production method.

## What this means for product teams

- Formulate minors as ratio partners in proven formats first. The evidence across BDSA tracking, Headset's October 2026 data and the 2026 launch record points the same way: gummies carry roughly 70–75% of minor-cannabinoid sales, and the winning SKUs name a ratio — THC/CBD/CBN, THC/CBG/THCV, CBD:CBG — rather than a lone minor. Tablets and softgels are the credible second format, as the Ascend and Canopy launches show.

- Write the production method into every ingredient specification. "Extracted from the plant" and "converted outside the plant" are now different legal goods with different federal dates. Require suppliers to state and document the method — extraction, semi-synthesis from a named precursor, or full synthesis — and keep the batch records with the certificate of analysis.

- Audit hemp-derived minor supply against December 11, 2026, not November 12. CBN, CBG and THCV are naturally producible, so the November date does not reach them by identity; converted supply and any finished hemp product above 0.4 mg of total THC per container lose hemp status on December 11. Requalify, reformulate, or move affected SKUs into licensed channels before that date.

- Build THCV plans around scarcity. At typical yields below 0.2% in most plants, THCV is a constrained input: secure cultivar-specific extraction supply, verify content on the batch certificate of analysis rather than the cultivar name, and do not base a Washington or similarly restrictive state's plan on converted THCV, which that state's licensed market prohibits.

- Use California's CBN isolate lane deliberately — and only as specified. AB 8 preserves CBD and CBN isolate above 99% purity with no THC and no synthetic cannabinoids for foods and beverages in the hemp program. That is a narrow, documented lane, not a general hemp exemption; anything with detectable THC belongs in the licensed system now, ahead of full integration on January 1, 2028.

- Keep the claims line where the evidence is. Ratio and content labelling is what the market leaders share; outcome claims are not supported by the current human literature, which the Washington LCB describes as limited and largely preclinical for THCV. Differentiate on format fit, ratio clarity and documented sourcing — the attributes a buyer can verify on the label and the certificate of analysis.

### Go deeper — the dataset behind this brief

Several figures in this brief come from BDSA retail sales tracking. If your team needs the underlying dataset — category, brand, and market-level sales to cut your own roadmap numbers — BDSA (https://bdsa1.referralrock.com/l/TAYLORAUGU09/) is the source the research cites. Research Brief · Market Intelligence

# New-State Market Entry 2026–2027: Reading Maturity Before Capital

Published November 11, 2026 · CannActuality Research Desk · For licensed vendors and product teams

### Key takeaways

- "Recently launched" covers very different markets. New York and Missouri already show diversified category mixes and more than 3.5 open retailers per 100,000 residents. Delaware had 13 stores open in March 2026 for a population of about 1.06 million.

- Price compression is now measurable in the larger young markets. Headset's average item price fell 9.5% year over year in New York and 7.6% in Ohio (October 2026), even though sales in both states grew.

- Flower share is the quickest signal of maturity. It ranges from about 32% of tracked sales in New York to roughly 55% in Delaware's first month and about 59% in Minnesota once shake and trim are included.

- Virginia is the next large launch. Retail sales are set for July 1, 2027, under a cap of 350 retail licenses, and applications are expected from February 2027. Pennsylvania has not legalized adult use; cannabis was left out of the budget signed in July 2026.

## Why score maturity before committing capital

Entrants often size a new-state launch from headline sales. Headline sales show how big a market is, not how open it is. Two states with similar annual revenue can need very different portfolios. One may still be short of supply and flower-led, so a narrow core range sells through. The other may be crowded and discounting, so every SKU has to hold its place on a shelf it shares with dozens of rivals. This brief scores six live adult-use markets on three signals a product team can check from public data, then adds the structural context (license caps, tax and timeline) that changes how fast a market will move from one stage to the next.

## The rubric

Each state gets 1 to 3 points on each signal. A higher score means a more mature, more contested market.

- Category mix (flower share of sales). 1 = 50% or more; 2 = 40–50%; 3 = under 40%. A falling flower share means consumers are spreading spend across vapes, pre-rolls and edibles, and that shelf space for formats has been claimed.

- Price compression (average item price, year over year). 1 = decline of 3% or less, or no published trend; 2 = decline of 3–7%; 3 = decline of more than 7%. Only percent changes are used.

- Retail density (open or approved retailers per 100,000 residents). 1 = under 1.5; 2 = 1.5–3.0; 3 = over 3.0. Population is the U.S. Census Bureau's Vintage 2025 estimate of total residents for July 1, 2025. That includes residents under 21, so these figures run lower than per-adult measures.

A total of 3–4 reads as Early (supply-constrained, flower-led), 5–6 as Developing, and 7–9 as Mature (diversified and compressing). Headset figures cover Headset-tracked retail sales for October 2026, not every sale in a state. Where a state publishes no price trend, the state scores 1 and is marked provisional.

## Scorecard: six live adult-use markets

 StateFlower shareAvg item price YoYRetailers per 100kScore
 New York32.4% (3)−9.5% (3)3.72 (3)9 · Mature
 Missouri39.4% (3)−3.2% (2)3.54 (3)8 · Mature
 Ohio46.9% (2)−7.6% (3)1.96 (2)7 · Mature
 Maryland47.4% (2)−4.9% (2)1.85 (2)6 · Developing
 Minnesota59.1% incl. shake/trim (1)Not published (1*)2.62 (2)4 · Early*
 Delaware55% (1)Not published (1*)1.23 (1)3 · Early*

* Provisional: no published price trend was found in the sources opened for this brief.

## Inputs behind the scores

Category mix. Shares for New York, Missouri, Ohio and Maryland are CannActuality's calculations from Headset's October 2026 category sales divided by each state's tracked total ($173.67 million, $134.11 million, $121.36 million and $105.19 million). Headset's Ohio page does not list pre-rolls, and the categories it does list add up to about 89% of the Ohio total. Minnesota's share comes from trailing 12-month figures from the Office of Cannabis Management, reported by The Marijuana Herald: flower $93 million plus shake and trim $23 million out of $196.07 million. Delaware's comes from the state's first-month release, in which flower was 55% of $7.35 million in sales.

Retail density. Each figure divides a retailer count by the Census Vintage 2025 population and multiplies by 100,000:

- New York: 744 open licensed dispensaries (Governor's office, Oct. 27, 2026) ÷ 20,002,427.

- Missouri: 222 approved dispensary licenses, from July figures in the state market study (Missouri Independent via KCUR, Oct. 27, 2026) ÷ 6,270,541.

- Ohio: 233 dual-use dispensary certificates of operation (Division of Cannabis Control, updated Oct. 26, 2026) ÷ 11,900,510.

- Maryland: 116 licensed dispensaries (Capital News Service, May 12, 2026; Maryland Matters reported 99 non-social-equity and 17 social equity stores operating on July 14, 2026) ÷ 6,265,347.

- Minnesota: 153 adult-use retailers (OCM data via The Marijuana Herald, June 3, 2026) ÷ 5,830,405. This leaves out 23 medical dispensaries.

- Delaware: 13 adult-use stores open (MJBizDaily, Mar. 12, 2026) ÷ 1,059,952.

Price compression. Headset states the New York (−9.5%) and Ohio (−7.6%) declines directly. The Maryland (−4.9%) and Missouri (−3.2%) figures are CannActuality's calculations from the current and year-ago average item prices on Headset's pages. Separately, MJBizDaily reported in August 2026 that Ohio's regulator-tracked flower price was down about 30% since the August 2024 launch but roughly flat over the prior year. That suggests Ohio's recent compression is coming from mix and non-flower formats rather than from flower.

## Structure: caps, taxes and timelines

 StateRetail tax (as reported)License pipeline or capSales momentum
 New York9% state + 4% local retail excise, plus a distributor-level tax1,039 licensed retailers, 744 openTracked sales +13.3% YoY (Oct. 2026)
 Missouri6% state; one local tax of up to 3% (no stacking)Constitutional floor of 24 dispensary licenses per congressional district; 144 microbusiness licenses expectedTracked sales +4.6% YoY; Nov. 2025 sales −2.6% YoY
 Ohio10% marijuana tax + 5.75% state sales tax233 dual-use dispensaries; 47 provisional licenses; about 137 local moratoriumsTracked sales +27.3% YoY
 Maryland12% sales and use tax (from 9% on July 1, 2025)83 social equity dispensary licenses awarded since 2023; 17 operating by July 2026Tracked sales +4.8% YoY
 Minnesota15% gross receipts tax + 6.875% sales tax + localLocal governments must allow at least one retailer per 12,500 residentsAbout $250 million in first-year sales (about $150 million adult-use)
 Delaware15%Up to 30 adult-use stores; 16 conditional retail licenses not yet open (March 2026)$53.4 million in the first year

The pipeline column matters as much as the score. New York has about 295 licensed retailers that are not yet open, which points to further density gains and more price pressure. Maryland's social equity cohort is only starting to open. Delaware can more than double its store count under its cap, and Minnesota's own regulator once estimated the state would need no fewer than 381 dispensaries. In those states, an Early score describes today's market, not the one a 2027 launch will meet.

## The next launches: Virginia and Pennsylvania

Virginia. Lawmakers passed a retail framework in March 2026. The retail start date was then set at July 1, 2027, through budget bill HB 30, which the Marijuana Policy Project described as signed on June 30, 2026. The framework allows up to 350 retail licenses, allocated by geographic zone. The Cannabis Control Authority is due to finalize regulations and begin taking applications by February 1, 2027, and must issue at least 55 further licenses by July 1, 2027. The state tax starts at 6% and rises to 8% after July 1, 2029, and localities may add 1–3.5%. The framework also caps THC at 10 mg per serving and 100 mg per package, a format constraint to design for from the start. At the full cap, Virginia would reach 3.94 retailers per 100,000 residents (350 ÷ 8,880,107). That is in the range of New York's and Missouri's density today, although it will take time to build.

Pennsylvania. Adult-use cannabis was left out of the budget Governor Shapiro signed in July 2026. A bipartisan bill was sent back to the Senate committee where it had stalled, according to MJBizDaily (July 13, 2026). None of the sources opened for this brief shows an enacted law or a launch timeline.

## What this means for product teams

- Match portfolio breadth to the score. In Early markets (Delaware, Minnesota), a narrow, flower-led core that you can keep in stock is likely to beat a wide range on thin supply. In Mature markets (New York, Missouri, Ohio), launch with vapes and pre-rolls in the core range, since together they already account for about half of tracked sales in New York.

- Price the launch on the trend, not the snapshot. In New York and Ohio, average item prices fell 7–10% in a year while sales grew. Model margins on next year's shelf, and build entry, core and premium tiers into the launch range.

- Read the license pipeline before you trust low density. Unopened licenses in New York, Maryland and Delaware mean today's density understates the competition you will face within 12–24 months.

- Treat Virginia as a 2027 regulatory project. Packaging and serving limits, zone-based retail allocation and a February 2027 rules deadline leave little time. Design compliant SKUs before applications open, not after.

- Re-score every quarter. All three signals come from public monthly data. A state can move a full band in a year, as Ohio's +27% sales growth alongside a −7.6% price trend shows.
